reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a purported Ethereum arbitrage or sniper bot as a passive-income tool, claiming massive daily profits and a 40% profit in 12 hours. It instructs viewers to use MetaMask, copy linked code into Remix, deploy a contract while paying gas fees, and fund it with Ethereum, while tying larger deposits to larger claimed profits. The promised return of the initial Ethereum plus profit relies on an unverified mechanism involving front-running, mempool sniping, and sandwiching transactions.

citations.quote: In today's video I'll show you how to set up an Ethereum trading bot I recently developed in the Solidity language, which I use to generate massive daily profits.
So, now we are going to deploy the smart contract.
the next step is to fund the contract with some Aetherium to snipe liquidity pools

You can fund the contract with however many Ethereum you want, but obviously the more you put in the larger the transactions you'll be able to snipe and the more profit you'll be able to accumulate over time.
This is going to enable us to front run, or snipe, transactions on decentralized finance exchanges such as Uniswap and PancakeSwap.

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker does not present returns as fixed or guaranteed: profits can fluctuate. He also tells viewers to check the token address rather than simply trust his claim. Those cautions matter when assessing whether the profit figures are a promise to viewers or an account of his own reported results. They do not prove the bot works, but the record supports a reading of a trading-tool demonstration with uncertain returns.

citations.quote: Profits will however fluctuate week-to-week.
Yep, as you can see it's the official wrapped Ether address – always check that.
So I generated a little over .7 Ethereum running my bot for just over 24 hours.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening points to a striking 12-hour return, but a reported result is not itself a guaranteed future return. Nor does explaining transaction ordering establish that the speaker conceals the nature of the proposed trade. His express acknowledgment that profits fluctuate limits the certainty the opening attributes to the pitch.

citations.quote: which is about 40% profit in only 12 hours.
Profits will however fluctuate week-to-week.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A brief fluctuation caveat does not undo the central appeal: the speaker claims massive daily profits, tells viewers to fund the contract, and says a larger deposit permits larger profits. Checking a token address does not verify what the linked bot code does or substantiate the claimed returns.

citations.quote: which I use to generate massive daily profits.

You can fund the contract with however many Ethereum you want, but obviously the more you put in the larger the transactions you'll be able to snipe and the more profit you'll be able to accumulate over time.
Yep, as you can see it's the official wrapped Ether address – always check that.

opening.argument: Judge, this is substantially a walkthrough of a Solidity workflow. The speaker directs viewers to create a file, paste source code, match the compiler version, and deploy a contract; he then describes what a contract control is supposed to do. Those concrete programming and operational steps support treating the video as a technology demonstration, even while its profit claims deserve skepticism. A tutorial can describe an ambitious use case without its demonstration alone establishing a deceptive solicitation.

citations.quote: Then click New File. We're going to name it bot.sole.
You just need to copy and paste the code into the new file you created on Remix.
Under Compiler we are going to select the version of 0.6.6 so it matches our contract.
Withdrawal will stop the bot and transfer the funds back to your wallet.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution accurately identifies instructions to fund the contract, but that step appears within the described deployment sequence, followed by a stated withdrawal step. Its opening treats a tutorial's funding instruction as decisive without showing, from that instruction alone, that the speaker controls viewers' deposits or that withdrawal is impossible.

citations.quote: so the next step is to fund the contract with some Aetherium to snipe liquidity pools
When you press withdraw, the bot will stop sniffing the mempool, and it will send the total Ethereum you sent initially, plus the profit back to your wallet.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The tutorial format is precisely how viewers are led from copying linked code to paying deployment fees and funding a contract. The claimed withdrawal function is the speaker's assertion, not proof that viewers can recover funds. The video ties that workflow to extraordinary reported returns, making the operational detail part of the pitch rather than evidence against it.

citations.quote: if you look in the description, I provided a link to the source code of my bot on GitHub. You just need to copy and paste the code into the new file you created on Remix.
the next step is to fund the contract with some Aetherium to snipe liquidity pools
which is about 40% profit in only 12 hours.

opening.argument: Judge, the described transaction is funding a smart contract that the viewer deploys, not an explicit request to send money to the speaker. The speaker says viewers can choose how much to fund it with and describes a withdrawal control that returns the initial funds along with any profit. That does not establish the contract is safe, but the supplied narrative does not identify the speaker as the recipient of the deposit or demonstrate that the stated withdrawal fails. The narrower reading is a promoted trading tool with unverified performance claims, not a demonstrated diversion of viewers' funds.

citations.quote: We see the transaction has confirmed and our contract is now deployed.
You can fund the contract with however many Ethereum you want
When you press withdraw, the bot will stop sniffing the mempool, and it will send the total Ethereum you sent initially, plus the profit back to your wallet.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution's strongest point is that viewers are told to fund a contract after copying linked code. That warrants scrutiny, but its opening does not establish what that code does with deposits or identify a destination controlled by the speaker. The account also includes a claimed return of funds to the wallet. The funding instruction alone cannot settle the contract's actual behavior.

citations.quote: I provided a link to the source code of my bot on GitHub.
This contract has one Ethereum in its balance which is the amount we funded the contract with.
it will send the total Ethereum you sent initially, plus the profit back to your wallet.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: An explicit admission of where diverted funds go is not necessary to recognize the risk in this pitch. Viewers are directed to copy the speaker's linked code, deploy it, and fund the resulting contract; the speaker links larger deposits to larger profits. His description of a withdrawal button does not verify the code or prove that deposits are recoverable.

the next step is to fund the contract with some Aetherium to snipe liquidity pools
